claims.text: In situ aberration-corrected TEM with a heating stage can directly observe thermally induced structural rearrangements in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles at atomic scale.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The initial nanoparticles have an ordered crystalline structure at room temperature.
High vacuum or a controlled inert atmosphere will prevent oxidation during heating.
Atomic interfaces, grain boundaries, and possible elemental-segregation regions may evolve with temperature.
Increasing thermal energy will induce atomic diffusion in the nanoparticles.
Increasing thermal energy will induce phase rearrangements in the nanoparticles.
Increasing thermal energy may induce subtle lattice distortions that are observable by AC-TEM.
Thermally induced atomic and structural changes underpin the predicted enhanced thermal stability of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
The experiment should reveal temperature-dependent atomic rearrangements or phase transitions.
The observed rearrangements or phase transitions will correlate with theories of improved thermal stability in high-entropy nanoparticles.
At room temperature, the nanoparticles have no significant thermal activation.
Electron-beam damage may limit observation of nanoparticle thermal behavior.
Instrumental resolution at very high temperatures may limit observation.
Some thermally induced structural changes may fall below the experiment's detection threshold.
The temperature at which significant atomic-scale rearrangements occur and the nature of the transitions are presently uncertain.

contradictions.description: The falsification rule treats a null observation as falsifying the method's ability to capture thermal modifications, while the boundary explicitly concedes that real changes may be hidden by beam damage or fall below detection limits. Thus, a null result cannot decisively distinguish structural stability from inadequate detectability.
